For if the resistance *DK* is uniform, the figure *BKTa* will be a rectangle under *Ba* and *DK*; and thus the rectangle under $\frac{1}{2} Ba$ and *Aa* will be equal to the rectangle under *Ba* and *DK*, and *DK* will be equal to $\frac{1}{2} Aa$. Therefore, since *DK* is the exponent of the resistance, and the length of the pendulum is the exponent of gravity, the resistance to gravity will be as $\frac{1}{2} Aa$ to the length of the pendulum; exactly as demonstrated in prop. xxviii.

If the resistance is as the velocity, the figure *BKTa* will be an ellipse very closely. For if a body, in a non-resisting medium, were to describe the length *BA* in one complete oscillation, the velocity at any point *D* would be as the ordinate *DE* applied to the diameter *AB* of the circle. Therefore, since *Ba* in a resisting medium and *BA* in a non-resisting medium are described in approximately equal times; and therefore the velocities at individual points of *Ba* are very nearly as the velocities at the corresponding points of the length *BA*, as *Ba* is to *BA*; the velocity at point *D* in a resisting medium will be as the ordinate applied to the circle or ellipse described upon the diameter *Ba*; and therefore the figure *BKVT a* will be an ellipse very closely. Since the resistance is supposed to be proportional to the velocity, let *OV* be the exponent of the resistance at the midpoint *O*; and the ellipse *BRVSa*, with center *O* and semi-axes *OB*, *OV*, will equal the figure *BKVT a*, and the rectangle *Aa* x *BO* equal to it, very closely. Therefore *Aa* x *BO* is to *OV* x *BO* as the area of this ellipse is to *OV* x *BO*: that is, *Aa* to *OV* as the area of a semicircle is to the square of the radius, or as 11 to 7 approximately: And therefore $\frac{7}{11} Aa$ is to the length of the pendulum as the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity.

But if the resistance *DK* is in the squared ratio of the velocity, the figure *BKVT a* will be nearly a parabola having *V* as its vertex and *OV* as its axis, and therefore will be equal to the rectangle under $\frac{2}{3} Ba$ and *OV* very closely. Therefore, the rectangle under $\frac{1}{2} Ba$ and *Aa* is equal to the rectangle under $\frac{2}{3} Ba$ and *OV*, and therefore *OV* is equal to $\frac{3}{4} Aa$: and therefore the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity as $\frac{3}{4} Aa$ is to the length of the pendulum.

You shall carry a dog’s tongue placed in your shoe under your big toe, or if you carry a dried dog’s heart with you, according to Sextus. Use hare hair or excrement, according to Pliny. Or, you shall carry the severed tail of a young weasel on your foot, or give a frog to the dog in a morsel of food; all these things serve to avoid the barking of dogs. Nigidius says that dogs will flee from the sight of a person all day if he expels a tick from a pig and carries it for a while. Oppian writes:

> If you carry a little piece cut from the skin of a hyena,
> Immediately the whelps and fierce dogs,
> Struck with bitter terror, will not bark at you
> As you walk past, even if they were barking before.

### That a dog cannot run.

If you smear its wings <note>Note: referring to the dog's legs/feet in the context of animal speed</note> with oil, it will be hindered in running; this is how it will happen.

### That a hawk may be spirited.

You will invigorate a bird against its prey so that it attacks large birds. Moisten the food it uses during the time of hunting with wine; or if it is a goshawk, give it a little vinegar. When you wish for it to fly, give it three morsels of meat soaked in wine, or pour wine into the beak of a pigeon chick, then make it fly. Thus,

### You will make partridges more combative,

If you give them branches of maidenhair fern <term>adiantum</term> <gloss>maidenhair fern</gloss> in their food, according to Pliny. And,

### Roosters become more combative,

By giving them garlic in their food shortly before they are to fight, from which the term <term>eskorodismenoi</term> <gloss>garlic-stuffed</gloss> is most wittily derived in ancient comedy, that is, one who is seasoned with garlic as a term for someone who is vehement and overly inclined toward fighting.

### That a bird may not fly high.

Pluck the tail feathers that direct the course upward; thus, it will fly in a circle below. If you wish,

### That a bird may not be able to fly.

Cut the upper and lower tendons of the wing, and it remains unharmed; the bird will not fly. In this way, they do not escape from aviaries.

The sun itself illuminates the other stars not so much by the magnitude of its divine power as by its divinity and holiness. Believe, therefore, O Asclepius, that this is the second god, governing all things and illuminating all mundane beings, whether they are animate or inanimate. For if the world is a living creature, always having been, being, and destined to be, nothing in the world is mortal. Since every part of the living being, which is in the world itself—just as in one and the same ever-living animal—has no place for mortality, God himself must therefore be most full of life and eternity, if it is necessary for him always to live. The sun, therefore, just like the world, is everlasting; and thus it is the governor of vital things, or the constant companion and dispenser of all their vitality. God, therefore, is the everlasting governor of the living or vital things that are in the world, and the eternal dispenser of life itself. He has dispensed this once by an eternal law, providing life to all vital things in the manner which I shall now describe.

There is no doubt that, just as men can kill by divine permission, so too can they truly and really remove that member <note>referring to the phallus, a frequent subject in the *Malleus Maleficarum*</note> or others. But in such cases, demons do not operate through the witches of whom mention is now being made. Through this, the solution to the second point is also clear. But as for the argument that because God permits the generative power to be bewitched more [often] for the sake of something, therefore it is also permitted that such a member be truly and really removed, this does not hold because this does not happen by way of witchcraft, nor do witches even desire this when they perform such acts, since they do not have the power of restoring the member when they wish and know how. From which it is clear that it is removed not truly, but by the art of illusion. 

Regarding the third point, concerning the wife of Lot, we say: it was true and not by the art of illusion, but we are now speaking of the art of illusion. 

Regarding the fourth point, that demons can induce certain substantial forms and therefore can also remove them: it is said, concerning the magicians of Pharaoh, that they created true serpents. Demons can indeed produce certain effects around imperfect creatures with the aid of some other agent, which they cannot do around human beings, for whom God has greater care. According to that saying: "Is God concerned about oxen?" <note>1 Corinthians 9:9</note>. They can, however, always—as has been said—harm human beings truly and really by divine permission, or even by the art of illusion, and through this, the solution to the last argument is also clear.

Nor again can it exist in the thing that is seen, such as a woman appearing as a beast, because two substantial forms cannot exist in the same subject at the same time and place. Therefore, since that form of a beast which is seen can exist nowhere, no illusory deception in the eye of the seer can occur, since vision must necessarily be terminated by some form. 

Furthermore, if it is said that this form exists in the surrounding air, this cannot be; firstly, because air is not receptive to any form or figure; and secondly, because it cannot remain the same air around that person due to its fluidity, especially as it moves; and also because such a transformation would thus be seen by everyone, which does not happen, since demons do not seem to be able to deceive the visions of holy men at least. Furthermore, the visual sense or visual power is a passive power. But every passive thing is moved by an active thing proportionate to it. Now, the active thing proportionate to the sense is twofold. Likewise, take care not to err with <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>tin</gloss>, because of the difficulty of its reduction. If, when you place its calx into reduction, it happens that it does not reduce, but you find it in its former state or reduced to glass, do not judge its reduction to be impossible. We say that if you do not apply a great fire in the reduction of <term>Jupiter</term>, it will not reduce. If, however, you apply a great fire, it does not necessarily follow that it will reduce, but it is possible that it might be reduced to vitrification <note>the process of turning into a glass-like substance</note>. This is because <term>Jupiter</term> has a fugitive substance of mercury <note>original: "argenti uiui"</note> enclosed in the depth of its nature. If it endures a long delay in the fire, it will flee, and it will leave the body deprived of humidity, such that it is found more apt to be converted to vitrification than to the fusion of a metallic body. For everything deprived of its proper humidity gives no fusion except a vitrifying one. Therefore, it is necessary that you hasten to reduce it quickly with the most rapid force of fire. Otherwise, it will not be reduced. Practice this, therefore, and you will know.

The second mode of calcination for these two bodies, <term>Saturn</term> <gloss>lead</gloss> and <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>tin</gloss>, which is perfected by the sharpness of salt, is that a quantity of salt be projected onto their surface, quantity by quantity, very often during their fusion, and mixed by much agitation with an iron rod over the fire, until they are turned into ash by the mixture of salt. And afterwards, their calx is to be perfected by the same mode of perfection, with its own considerations. But there is also a difference in the calcination of these two bodies. Because <term>lead</term> is converted into powder more easily from the initial labors of calcination than <term>Jupiter</term>, yet its calx is not perfected more easily than that of <term>Jupiter</term>. The cause of this depends on the fact that <term>Saturn</term> has a more fixed humidity than <term>Jupiter</term>.

For Plato believes that vision is formed according to clarity, specifically through light flowing out from the eyes toward an external air, and light from bodies being carried to meet it. This light, which exists in the intervening air, is easily extended alongside the fire-like faculty of sight, which is capable of being poured forth and turned. Galen agrees with Plato, but Hipparchus claims that rays extended from the eyes reach out to bodies, touching them as if with a certain palpitation, and thus render their perception to the sight. The Epicureans, however, affirm that images of what appears force themselves upon the eyes. Aristotle, on the other hand, believes that images are not bodies themselves, but that the quality comes from visible objects to the sight through an alteration of the air that surrounds us. Yet geometers and opticians, leaning somewhat toward Hipparchus, propose certain cones formed by the coincidence of rays emitted through the eyes. ### PROCESS LXXVII.
**Tincture of Tartarized Tartar.**

#### APPARATUS.
Take Tartarized Tartar, duly prepared according to Process 75 and dried, then ground into a fine powder. Pour over it in a tall chemical vial the purest alcohol of wine, to a height of four inches above the powder. Then, with the vial closed only by paper, let them boil together as gently as possible in our wooden furnace for the space of twenty-four hours. The alcohol will be of a golden color, floating on top, with an aromatic odor and a penetrating, warm taste. If this is repeated with fresh alcohol in the same manner, a white salt will eventually be left at the bottom. The tinctures are thickened over a gentle fire so that a tenth part remains, concentrated at the bottom.

#### USE.
It serves to demonstrate the part in that salt which is dissolved by alcohol. The tincture itself, when prepared, is aromatic, warming, and consolidates ulcers and wounds. The remaining salt, being simpler than before, shows that salts themselves can be whitened once a tincture is extracted by the help of alcohol.

### PROCESS LXXVIII.
**Dissolution of Regenerated Tartar in Alcohol.**

#### APPARATUS.
Take regenerated tartar, prepared as cleanly as possible and with as much care as can be managed, in a tall, chemical, glass vial. Pour over it six times its volume of the purest alcohol and boil it over a gentle fire in our wooden furnace, as prudently as possible. They will combine with each other, and out of these, a single, uniformly composed substance will be formed, with impurities deposited at the bottom. After they have then settled accurately through quiet standing, let the supernatant and pure liquor flow out by a careful tilting of the vessel. If any saline matter that has not yet dissolved remains, it can be dissolved by the application of fresh alcohol with the same caution and separated from the dregs. Then indeed, let the prepared liquors be concentrated by distillation over a very gentle fire to half their volume; the tincture of this salt will be obtained.

#### USE.
You see in this experiment the bringing together into one of alkali, oily acid, the oil of spirits, and vegetables. Hence, the most active principles of plants are freed from inert earth, yet at the same time they are sufficiently safe and not excessively sharp or dangerous. These, indeed, so joined, seem to constitute even the small Elixir of the Sages, which the masters of the ancient Art recommended for preserving and restoring health. It heals almost all obstructions by flowing through the vessels, <column-break/>

In chemistry, it also provides a most effective solvent, by which substances are reduced to their smallest parts, active and with their seminal virtue unimpaired, so that they may be admitted into the inner chambers of the body to restrain and subdue any rebellious matter. Then he proceeds to what that weakness was: namely, that it had external justifications of the flesh which could not render its worshippers perfect in conscience, and that through the sacrifices of beasts, it could neither blot out sins nor procure true holiness. Article 3: Whether the more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

Regarding the third article, the procedure is as follows: It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition, because things that are prior by nature are posterior and less known to us, but universals are prior by nature. Furthermore, composite things are prior to us compared to simple things, but universals are simple; therefore, they are known later to us. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, *Physics* I</note> says that the defined <note>term: *diffinitum* <gloss>the thing defined</gloss></note> falls into our cognition before the parts of the definition, and parts of a definition are less universal; for instance, "animal" is a part of the definition of "man," yet universals are known later to us. Furthermore, we encounter effects and causes and principles <unclear>by chance</unclear>, but universals are known later to us. But if it is true that, as stated in the first book of the *Physics*, we proceed from the whole to the singulars, I respond that it must be said that in our intellectual cognition, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual cognition takes its origin in some way from sensory cognition. And because sense is of singulars, while the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars is prior to us than the cognition of universals. Second, we must consider that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. And what proceeds from potency to act arrives first at the incomplete act, which is midway between pure potency and perfect act. The perfect act, to which the intellect arrives, is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known as being in act and in a certain way in potency. As it is said in the first book of the *Physics*, what is first manifest and certain to us is more confused. Afterward, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly. It is manifest that to know something in which many things are contained, without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained within it, is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, a whole, or that in which parts are contained in potency, and an integral whole can be known; for both wholes can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. However, to know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have knowledge of a less common thing: just as knowing "animal" indistinctly versus knowing the animal in which rationality or irrationality exists, which is knowing a man or a lion. Therefore, it occurs to our intellect first to know "animal" and to know "man." And if I compare any thing, whether more or less, just as sense goes from potency to act, so does the intellect. Man does not know this, even though he calls his intellect "sight" and attributes light to it. Rather, this is what must be pursued: that through it, secrets may be uncovered, and the deceits of the <term>seplasiariorum</term> <gloss>apothecaries/perfumers</gloss>—by whom the rude masses are cheated while they are served for a single florin what would not be worth a single coin—may be exposed. Such are their precious secrets.

<margin>Poison exists even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who dares to deny that poison lies hidden and exists even in the best of things? Everyone is compelled to admit it. If this is true, I now ask of you: should poison not be separated from the good and useful, and the good accepted while the evil is left behind? Indeed, it must be so. If, therefore, it is necessary, I ask you to explain to me how this is separated in your workshops? For with you, everything remains mixed. But in order to defend your simplicity, if you are convicted into admitting that poison lies hidden there, and are asked where it eventually goes, you then produce something regarding "corrections" <note>referring to pharmaceutical methods intended to mitigate the toxicity of ingredients</note> that supposedly extract and remove the poison,
<margin>The correction of physicians is examined.</margin>
just as they correct Quince with Scammony, or as they say, Diagridium <note>a preparation of scammony resin</note>. But what kind of correction is that? Does the poison not remain afterwards just as it did at first? And yet, you boast meanwhile that you have corrected it, so that the poison no longer causes harm. Where, truly, has it vanished?
<margin>Diagridium.</margin>
It remains in the Diagridium. Try this, if you are wise: exceed the measure, and you will see where the poison is. For you will know it without delay. Thus you also correct Turbith <note>a purgative root</note>, and call it Diaturbith. Your corrections are of a kind that would suit peasants and should be fed to horses. Make a trial by exceeding the measure, and increase the dose: you will see if you do not feel the poison.
<margin>What it means to correct as a physician</margin>
*To correct is to take the corrected.* If a person is malicious and has sinned, if he is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of the one who has been punished endures. These corrections of yours are of the same kind; they depend on the substances themselves, not on you. Now, in this case, a physician must consider nothing more than that the poison be taken away. That must be done through separation. As, for example: a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted as food. If you remove the poison from it, you may eat it without harm. The same must be understood equally regarding all other things; namely, that a similar separation is needed. If that has not yet been done, you cannot be secure in your operation, unless it happens that nature supplies your failings, or the greater kindness of the heavens grants favor. For in your art, there will be no protection left.

Now, therefore, if that true foundation is required which removes the poison, how does Alchemy provide it? For it is necessary that it be done in such a way that, if Mars <note>iron</note> is in the Sun <note>gold</note>, the Mars must be removed; and if Saturn <note>lead</note> is dwelling in Venus <note>copper</note>, it must be separated from her. For as many ascendants and impressions as there are in the things of nature, so many bodies exist within them. Truly, as for those bodies that are contrary, it is necessary that some part of them be removed and taken away, so that in this manner all contrariety may be lifted, and the evil that you seek may be removed from the good.
<margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin>
Just as gold is useful for nothing unless it is first thrown into the fire, so much less useful is medicine that does not pass through the fire. For it is necessary for all things to pass through fire into a second generation, which ought to lead to and assist man. And should this not justly be considered the proper foundation of any physician? For a physician ought not to employ poisons, but true secrets.
<margin>Workshops criticized.</margin>
However, all those workshop preparations, as many as they are, do not contribute even a single letter to this teaching; rather, they are occupied simply in "correcting," just as if a dog had farted in a room, and that stench were suppressed either with lozenges and incense or with juniper wood: I ask, does the stench not remain in the room afterwards just as it did before? And even if it is not perceived by the sense of smell, is one therefore allowed to say that the stench has been separated and remains no longer? No, it is present, but corrected by fumigation. Thus, the fumigation and the stench enter the nostrils together. Such also are the corrections of apothecaries, who dull the <term>Aleopaticum</term> <gloss>a general term here for harsh or toxic medicaments</gloss> with sugar, so that it may inflict no harm. Thus, sugar and honey are their "mastery." They even correct gentian with theriac <note>an ancient medicinal antidote</note>. Are these not works of asinine ignorance? Yet they boast and sell themselves as the chief physicians. But who is so stupid that he does not smell immediately that these things are worthless? For what else can they boast of regarding their remedies, other than to say, *This electuary is sweet, made from aromatics, sugar, and honey.*
